stories.head: Voyager bags $16.5M DARPA contract for rockets
stories.body: Voyager has secured a $16.5 million DARPA contract aimed at developing thrust-control technology for solid rocket propulsion systems. This contract is intended to enhance adaptability across various missions, which might just make solid rockets a bit less... solid in their application. If successful, this could open the door for broader use in defense and commercial sectors.
stories.soWhat: If Voyager can deliver, we might see a shift in how solid propulsion is integrated into diverse missions, which could rattle the status quo in propulsion tech.

stories.head: True Anomaly raises $190M amid security concerns
stories.body: True Anomaly has closed a $190 million Series C round, pushing its valuation to $1.6 billion as it focuses on co-orbital security and space domain awareness. The funding reflects a growing recognition of the need for enhanced security in space, particularly as geopolitical tensions rise. This cash infusion will likely accelerate the development of their capabilities.
stories.soWhat: The defense pull-through is real; True Anomaly's success could signal a trend where security needs drive funding, overshadowing traditional innovation metrics.

stories.head: Europe's smallsat sector struggles with regulations
stories.body: Despite a proposed legislative overhaul, Europe's small satellite industry continues to be hampered by stringent regulations and limited access to capital. These challenges persist even as defense spending increases, indicating a disconnect between funding and operational flexibility. Companies in the sector are feeling the squeeze, with many calling for more supportive regulatory frameworks.
stories.soWhat: If Europe can't untangle its regulatory mess, it risks losing its competitive edge in the smallsat market to more agile players elsewhere.

talent.statLabel: Job orders YoY · plus 2 starters per head, an 8-year first
talent.head: Demand has doubled. So has our hit rate.
talent.body: EVONA's job orders are up 2.0× year-over-year, and for the first time in our eight-year history we're placing two new starters per EVONA staff member. The first number says demand is real. The second says we're converting it, which in recruitment is the only number that actually matters. Growth is heaviest in Series B/C startups; primes are running flat. Compensation isn't the variable. The constraint is schedule risk in the primes: senior engineers leave Boeing, Lockheed, Northrop because they want to ship hardware before retirement.
